chunks: Clock frequency, power and thermals. The question: How does clock frequency impact power, performance, and thermals?
Clock frequency is how many steps per second a chip takes. A faster clock gets more work done per second, but it uses more power, and that power turns into heat.
Faster clocks also need a higher supply voltage, so power grows faster than speed does.
Heat then limits how fast the chip can run for long, so chips slow themselves down when they get too hot.
Picture an assembly line. A faster belt makes more items per minute at the same energy each, so power rises in step with speed.
But past a certain speed, workers need overtime pay to keep up, and that makes every item cost more. Doubling the speed then costs more than double the power.
The factory also warms up, and a hot factory wastes more energy, which warms it further.
A purely compute-bound workload (m = 0) gets the full 2x; a workload that is half memory-bound gets only 1. 33x.
This is why raising the clock alone is a poor way to speed up memory-bound code, and why caches and memory bandwidth matter.
Clock frequency: the number of ticks per second, in hertz. The chip takes one step per tick.
Dynamic power: power spent on switching, equal to alpha C V squared f : the charge the flipping wires hold per volt ( alpha C ), times voltage squared, times frequency.
Leakage: power that flows even when nothing switches. It rises as the chip heats up. Thermal resistance ( theta ): how many degrees the chip warms per watt.
Throttling: lowering the clock so the chip stays cool. DVFS: changing voltage and frequency together to match the load.
Take a chip with alpha C = 20 nanofarads. At 2 gigahertz and 0. 9 volts, power is 20 times 10 to the -9 times 0. 9 squared times 2 times 10 to the 9 equals 32. 4 watts.
At 4 gigahertz it needs 1. 1 volts, so power is 20 times 10 to the -9 times 1. 1 squared times 4 times 10 to the 9 equals 96. 8 watts.
Twice the frequency costs about 3 times the power. With theta equals 0. 5 K/W (0.
5 degrees Celsius per watt) and a 45 degrees Celsius surrounding, the chip runs at about 61 degrees Celsius and then about 93 degrees Celsius. That is the whole idea.
"Dynamic power is alpha C V squared f , so at fixed voltage it's linear in frequency.
Performance also rises with frequency, but only for the part of the workload not waiting on memory.
The catch is that higher frequency needs higher voltage to meet timing, so along a DVFS curve power grows much faster than linearly, about 3x for 2x frequency in a typical example.
All that power becomes heat, T j equals T a plus P theta , and leakage rises with temperature, which can feed back into throttling.
That's why frequency is the main knob for managing power and thermals."
